lines.text: Marda's rumor board said the frogfolk still ferry the ones they like. A ferrywoman called Gullet likes you. Tonight, ride with her through the Whispering Marsh and find a way out. New wisps crowd behind bell ribbons.
"Too many,"
Gullet hums.
"Ask the boggarts. They keep lost things."
"Something's leaking,"
you say. The new wisps all turn toward you at once, like candles in a draft. Gullet carves a notch in her hat.
"Not near the wisps,"
she says.
"They remember things."
"Gems are the most lost things this season,"
Gullet hums, steering for the boggarts' island. A frog salutes from a lily pad. She salutes back, just in case.
Gullet's cousins are moving a bell ribbon across the channel. Their leader wears three hats. Help them and earn a dry crossing later, or duck under on your own.
"Never through it,"
Gullet says.
Jingle. Jingle-jingle. Every bell on the line goes off at once. The new wisps all crowd to the ribbon to see who rang, and the ribbon crew, all together, say
"Tsk."
Gullet poles away very fast, pretending she has never met you.
You hold the pole while the cousins retie their ribbon.
"Good hands,"
croaks the cousin in three hats.
"We will carry you across the weir later."
Your bigfoot crouches by the ribbon post. These are MossHome path-knots, tied by bigfoot to mean this way has moved.
"Tall lady with cords,"
says a cousin.
"Never stopped jogging."
A boggart called Nana Rummage sorts lost things on her island: mittens, umbrellas, a teapot lid. A bag hums in her lap.
"Trade, maybe,"
she tells a mitten. She wants an unusual sound.
Nana opens her bag. A gem chip hums one low note.
"Like the old Gate in the still water,"
she tells a teapot lid.
"The Hollow Gate. Exactly the same."
To an umbrella:
"Not that I said."
"Thank you,"
you tell the nearest umbrella. Nana is so pleased she nearly looks at you. She hands you a teapot lid, then takes it back. That is how boggarts say goodbye.
Nana answers the mitten instead.
"Barges are very convenient this season. Abandoned ones. Gem on the deck. Very, very convenient."
The mitten says nothing. What did she mean?
Nana tells the teapot lid what she found: umbrellas, a brown hat, and three prospectors.
"Barge spat them out. They're on a tussock north of here. Too loud for my collection."
Knotted reeds block the channel.
"Another toll,"
Gullet hums. A reed holds out its tip like a waiting hand. The knots tremble whenever somebody speaks.
A barge sits in the reeds. ABANDONED, says its very helpful sign. One gem hums on deck. Prospector footprints lead toward it. None come back.
"That is certainly a barge,"
Gullet hums.
"Very convenient,"
you say loudly, like Nana.
"An abandoned barge, with one gem on it."
A barnacle blinks. The whole barge sighs, unfolds into an embarrassed mire mimic, and slides into the reeds.
The barge has eyelashes. Barges do not have eyelashes.
"You're a mire mimic,"
you say, and the whole barge sighs, unfolds into something long and muddy and embarrassed, and slides off into the reeds.
Your kitsune circles the barge, nose in the air.
"Barnacles on the wrong side. That rope is a tail. And nobody abandons a polished lantern."
A wounded silence. The barge unfolds into a mire mimic and slinks off.
Gullet ties her raft to a lantern pole and fries duckweed fritters on a hot stone. They taste like crunchy pond.
"Rest a while,"
she hums. But fog is rolling in, thick as porridge.
Gullet turns her hat around. Every notch is a new wisp since the mountain went off. The brim is full.
"When I run out of hat,"
she says,
"I'll start on my other hat."
Fog hides the channel fork and its stumps.
"Which way, then?"
Gullet hums. Follow a clear gap from the bow, steer by the bells behind you, or risk the wobbly high pole.
"Stump left! Stump right! Heron!"
You call them all, and Gullet threads the raft through like a needle through cloth. From the top of the pole you spot something else, too: a little island ahead, with people standing on it.
Three muddy prospectors balance on a sinking tussock.
"Barge kept my good hat,"
says the tallest. Bring them aboard, and they may help you later. Or guide them out through the shallows.

One heave, two heaves, and all three slide aboard like wet sacks of flour. The raft rides very low. Gullet drops them at a frogfolk landing where a path leads northeast toward the roads, and the tallest one gives you a squashed honeycake.
"For the rescue. Sorry about the squash."
"Nana Rummage has your hat,"
you say. The tallest gasps. Gullet sighs and poles them back to Nana's island for it. Then she drops them by a path to the northeast roads.
You point out the sandy shallows. The prospectors wade off and wave from safety.
"Going home!"
calls the tallest.
"The rush can keep my hat."
"Please."
The wisp goes pink, then gold. Nobody has asked it politely before. It glows in front of your face, ready to share a memory.
Nana rows up in a washtub, paddling with a soup ladle.
"Lost things drift here. More lately,"
she tells it. She fishes out a surprised fish, puts it back, and waits for your question.
"The trees keep lost things too,"
Nana tells the ladle.
"Not mittens. Humming things."
She sniffs at their poor taste and rows backward into the fog.
"Everybody on the roads is going the same way,"
Nana tells a spoon.
"None of them knows they are lost."
She rows backward into the fog.
At the rush road, a sausage cart is stuck to its axles.
"Free sausages for help!"
pants the seller. A goose honks on behalf of the whole waiting line.
You carpet the mud with reeds. The cart rolls free.
"Clever marsh folk!"
shouts the seller, and hands over supper. The goose takes the credit.
"Tussock people!"
Your prospectors run from the line to push. The cart shoots free, and the seller brings back supper for everyone. The tallest prospector gets an extra sausage.
The cousin in three hats spots you.
"The good hands!"
the cousins cry. They carry your raft across on their shoulders, singing, and set you down dry on the north bank. Gullet pretends not to be proud.
A crowd of new wisps follows your raft, bumping it like puppies.
"Keep them busy till the island!"
calls the cousin in three hats.
"Bored wisps tie knots. Last week they tied my hats together."
The reeds keep swinging shut, like doors in a draft.
"Wait for it,"
Gullet hums.
"Wait. Now!"
Pole through when the gap is wide.
Gullet passes the lantern forward while you steady its hook. The fog stops at the edge of its glow like a shy cat.
"Good hands,"
she says, and puts a jar of mosslight in your pack.
"Fog gets thick past here."
Somebody on the island ahead is grumbling. But first comes the biggest stump yet, rolling like a sleeping cow.
"Fend it off!"
hums Gullet.
"Push when it rolls close. Not before!"
The crabs scuttle into deep water and leave their heap. Gullet picks through it with her pole.
"Spoons are Nana's. This whistle is nobody's."
She tosses you a very loud tin whistle.
Jingle-jingle! Every bell goes off. The ribbon crew all say
"Tsk."
Gullet poles away fast.
They slide aboard like wet sacks of flour. Gullet drops them by a path to the northeast roads. The tallest gives you a squashed honeycake.
"Sorry about the squash."
The wisps sway together, glowing slow and gold. They settle into a soft line behind the raft.
"Three coins for the calm,"
says the cousin in three hats.
The wisps follow the cattails with their whole bodies. They settle into a soft line behind the raft.
"Three coins for the calm,"
says the cousin in three hats.
The wisps circle it, politely, like moths with manners. They settle into a soft line behind the raft.
"Three coins for the calm,"
says the cousin in three hats.
The barnacle blinks first. It has eyelashes.
"Mire mimic!"
you say. The barge unfolds and slinks into the reeds. You never had to step aboard.
The whole deck rises, then holds its breath.
"Mire mimic!"
you say. The barge unfolds and slinks into the reeds. You never had to step aboard.
The rope twitches. It is a tail, having a difficult day.
"Mire mimic!"
you say. The barge unfolds and slinks away. You never had to step aboard.
